stem: Which set of findings meets the 2024 consensus diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.A: Blood ketones of 0.8 mmol/L with pH 7.32
options.B: Glucose above 33.3 mmol/L with effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and an arterial pH of 7.35
options.C: Glucose of 8 mmol/L with normal bicarbonate
options.D: Glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L or known diabetes, ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L, and pH <7.3 and/or HCO3− <18
options.E: Glucose above 13.9 mmol/L with lactate above 4 mmol/L

explanation: The 2024 international consensus defines DKA by hyperglycaemia (≥200 mg/dL) or a history of diabetes, ketonaemia (β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L) or significant ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18). The lower glucose threshold recognises euglycaemic DKA.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: What is the standard IV insulin regimen for adult DKA?

options.A: Long-acting insulin glargine IV
options.C: Insulin only once glucose exceeds 30 mmol/L, given as hourly subcutaneous rapid-acting boluses
options.E: Fixed-rate IV regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/h, with or without a 0.1 units/kg bolus

explanation: Continuous IV insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h suppresses ketogenesis and lowers glucose; an initial bolus is optional. Subcutaneous rapid-acting analogues are an alternative in mild–moderate DKA. Long-acting basal insulin may be continued subcutaneously to facilitate transition.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: A patient with DKA has an initial serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L. What should be done before starting insulin?

options.A: Give sodium bicarbonate
options.B: Give an insulin bolus and recheck the potassium level in 6 hours
options.C: Withhold insulin and give IV potassium until K+ is ≥3.5 mmol/L
options.E: Start insulin immediately at 0.1 U/kg/h

explanation: Insulin drives potassium into cells; starting it with K+ below 3.5 mmol/L risks fatal arrhythmias and respiratory muscle weakness. Despite normal or high initial levels, total body potassium is depleted in DKA; replacement is added to fluids when K+ is below 5.0–5.5 mmol/L with adequate urine output.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: During DKA treatment, glucose falls to 12 mmol/L (216 mg/dL) while ketones remain 3.5 mmol/L and pH 7.20. What is the appropriate adjustment?

options.A: Switch to subcutaneous insulin immediately
options.B: Reduce insulin to 0.01 U/kg/h and stop all IV fluids until the glucose rises again
options.C: Add dextrose (5–10%) to IV fluids and continue insulin to clear ketones
options.E: Give bicarbonate

explanation: Glucose normalises before ketoacidosis resolves. The 2024 consensus recommends adding dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) and continuing insulin until ketoacidosis resolves, preventing hypoglycaemia and allowing ketone clearance.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: Which criteria define resolution of DKA according to the 2024 consensus?

options.A: Ketones <0.6 mmol/L and venous pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L
options.B: Normal anion gap with persistent ketonaemia of 2 mmol/L
options.E: Disappearance of urinary ketones

explanation: Resolution requires ketones below 0.6 mmol/L plus pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18 mmol/L. Urine ketones lag behind blood ketones because acetoacetate (detected by nitroprusside) increases as β-hydroxybutyrate is metabolised.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: When transitioning a patient from IV insulin to subcutaneous basal–bolus insulin after DKA resolution, what is recommended?

options.A: Switch to oral hypoglycaemic agents only
options.B: Stop IV insulin and give the first subcutaneous dose about 6 hours later with a meal
options.C: Continue IV insulin for 72 hours after resolution
options.D: Overlap: give subcutaneous basal insulin 1–2 hours before stopping IV insulin
options.E: Give subcutaneous insulin only at the next meal

explanation: IV insulin has a half-life of minutes; stopping it without prior subcutaneous basal insulin causes rebound hyperglycaemia and recurrent ketoacidosis. Basal insulin should be given 1–2 hours before stopping IV insulin; early basal insulin during treatment is also acceptable.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: In adult DKA, when is sodium bicarbonate considered?

options.A: When glucose exceeds 30 mmol/L
options.C: In all patients with pH below 7.3
options.E: To speed ketone clearance

explanation: Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA with pH ≥7.0 and may cause hypokalaemia, paradoxical CNS acidosis and delayed ketone clearance. The 2024 consensus suggests considering it only when pH is below 7.0.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: A patient taking empagliflozin presents 2 days after surgery with vomiting, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, ketones 5.5 mmol/L and glucose 9.5 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
options.B: Starvation ketosis requiring no insulin, only oral intake
options.D: Euglycaemic DKA associated with SGLT2 inhibitor therapy
options.E: Lactic acidosis from metformin

explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors promote glycosuria, glucagon secretion and ketogenesis, causing DKA with near-normal glucose, especially with surgery, fasting or reduced insulin doses. Treatment requires IV insulin with dextrose from the start, and the SGLT2 inhibitor should be stopped (and withheld 3–4 days before surgery).
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: An elderly patient has glucose 50 mmol/L (900 mg/dL), Na+ 150 mmol/L, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L and ketones 0.8 mmol/L. What is the effective serum osmolality and diagnosis?

options.A: 300 mOsm/kg; mild hyperglycaemia without HHS
options.E: 450 mOsm/kg; HHS

explanation: Effective osmolality = 2 × Na+ + glucose = 2 × 150 + 50 = 350 mOsm/kg. HHS is defined by marked hyperglycaemia (≥600 mg/dL), effective osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg (or total above 320), and absence of significant ketoacidosis (pH ≥7.3, bicarbonate ≥15, ketones below 3.0).
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]; Mustafa et al. 2023 (JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) [144]

stem: In HHS, what is the recommended initial approach to fluids and insulin?

options.A: Use fluid restriction to prevent cerebral oedema
options.B: Aim to normalise sodium within 6 hours
options.C: Start insulin at 0.1 U/kg/h with a bolus before any IV fluids are given, to lower glucose quickly
options.D: Give hypotonic 0.45% saline as the initial fluid
options.E: Start with IV 0.9% saline; add low-dose insulin (0.05 U/kg/h) once glucose stops falling

explanation: JBDS recommends fluid replacement first, because fluids alone lower glucose and osmolality; early insulin causes rapid osmotic shifts. Insulin at 0.05 U/kg/h is added when glucose stops falling or with significant ketonaemia. The target fall in osmolality is 3–8 mOsm/kg/h.
referenceText: Mustafa et al. 2023 (JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) [144]

stem: Which complication is particularly common in HHS and should be prevented in all patients unless contraindicated?

options.A: Hypothyroidism
options.C: Acute pancreatitis in all patients, requiring daily lipase
options.E: Venous thromboembolism; prophylactic LMWH is recommended

explanation: HHS causes profound dehydration, hyperviscosity and immobility, increasing VTE risk. JBDS recommends prophylactic LMWH for the duration of admission unless contraindicated. Foot protection is also important because of pressure ulcer risk.
referenceText: Mustafa et al. 2023 (JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) [144]

stem: A young adult with DKA develops headache, bradycardia and declining consciousness 6 hours into treatment. What is the most likely complication and urgent treatment?

options.A: Meningitis; give antibiotics only and continue the current fluids
options.B: Cerebral oedema; give mannitol or hypertonic saline, slow fluids
options.E: Hypoglycaemia; give insulin

explanation: Cerebral oedema occurs mainly in children and young adults with DKA, often 4–12 hours into treatment, associated with rapid osmolality reduction. Treatment is mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg) or hypertonic saline, head elevation and reduction of fluid rate, with neuroimaging after stabilisation.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which statement about fluid choice in DKA is supported by recent evidence and the 2024 consensus?

options.A: Balanced crystalloids may resolve DKA faster than saline and are acceptable
options.B: Fluids should be withheld until the insulin infusion has been started and glucose is falling
options.D: Dextrose 5% is the initial fluid of choice
options.E: Hypotonic saline is mandatory initially

explanation: Secondary analyses of SMART and SALT-ED, and small trials, suggest faster resolution of DKA with balanced crystalloids, partly by avoiding hyperchloraemic acidosis. The 2024 consensus permits either isotonic saline or balanced crystalloids for initial resuscitation.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]; Semler et al. 2018 (SMART) [192]

stem: Which ECG change is characteristic of severe hypercalcaemia?

options.A: Peaked T waves
options.D: Prolonged QT interval with prominent U waves
options.E: Shortened QT interval, with possible bradyarrhythmias

explanation: Hypercalcaemia shortens the ST segment and QT interval and can cause bradycardia, AV block and, rarely, Osborn-like J waves. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT interval. Severe hypercalcaemia increases sensitivity to digoxin.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with intentional gliclazide overdose has recurrent hypoglycaemia despite repeated dextrose boluses. Which treatment reduces recurrence?

options.A: More concentrated dextrose boluses alone
options.E: Insulin infusion

explanation: Dextrose stimulates further insulin release from pancreatic beta cells primed by sulfonylureas, causing rebound hypoglycaemia. Octreotide (e.g. 50 µg subcutaneously every 6 hours) inhibits insulin secretion and reduces dextrose requirements. Glucagon has only a transient effect.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A patient with thyroid storm has fever 40 °C, AF at 160/min, agitation and heart failure. What is the correct order of initial drug therapy?

options.A: Aspirin for fever and no other therapy
options.B: Beta-blocker, then a thionamide (e.g. PTU), then iodine ≥1 hour later, plus corticosteroids
options.D: Iodine first, followed by a thionamide 1 hour later, and then a beta-blocker once rate-controlled
options.E: Radioactive iodine immediately

explanation: Thionamides must precede iodine by at least an hour to block organification of the iodine load (which otherwise provides substrate for new hormone synthesis). PTU also inhibits peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Corticosteroids reduce conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency; aspirin is avoided because it displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]

stem: Which scoring system is used to estimate the likelihood of thyroid storm?

options.A: CURB-65
options.E: APACHE II score

explanation: The Burch–Wartofsky Point Scale assigns points for temperature, CNS effects, GI–hepatic dysfunction, heart rate, heart failure, AF and a precipitating event; a score of 45 or more is highly suggestive of thyroid storm. The Japanese Thyroid Association criteria are an alternative.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]

stem: An elderly woman with untreated hypothyroidism presents with hypothermia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia and coma. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: IV hydrocortisone, then an IV levothyroxine loading dose (e.g. 200–400 µg)
options.B: Liothyronine 100 µg IV bolus without steroids
options.C: Rapid active external rewarming to 37 °C within 1 hour, then oral thyroxine
options.E: Oral levothyroxine 25 µg daily

explanation: Myxoedema coma has high mortality. ATA guidance recommends IV levothyroxine loading (200–400 µg) followed by daily IV replacement, with stress-dose hydrocortisone until coexisting adrenal insufficiency is excluded. Supportive care includes ventilation, passive rewarming and treatment of precipitants.
referenceText: Jonklaas et al. 2014 (ATA hypothyroidism) [106]

stem: A patient with prolonged septic shock has low free T3, low-normal free T4 and normal TSH. What is the appropriate management?

options.A: No replacement; this reflects non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid) syndrome
options.C: Start levothyroxine 100 µg daily via the nasogastric tube and recheck in 6 weeks
options.E: Start carbimazole

explanation: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome results from reduced peripheral deiodination and altered TSH secretion in critical illness. Low T3 correlates with severity, but thyroid hormone replacement has not improved outcomes. Thyroid tests should be repeated after recovery.
referenceText: Jonklaas et al. 2014 (ATA hypothyroidism) [106]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: The 2017 CIRCI guideline suggests which tests can be used to diagnose CIRCI when testing is performed?

options.A: Plasma renin activity
options.C: Delta cortisol <9 µg/dL after 250 µg cosyntropin, or random total cortisol <10 µg/dL
options.E: Free cortisol above 50 µg/dL with a raised plasma ACTH concentration on two separate occasions

explanation: The SCCM/ESICM CIRCI guideline suggests that CIRCI may be diagnosed by a delta cortisol (after 250 µg cosyntropin) below 9 µg/dL or a random plasma cortisol below 10 µg/dL, though neither test is highly reliable. Treatment decisions in septic shock depend mainly on vasopressor requirement.
referenceText: Annane et al. 2017 (CIRCI guideline) [9]

stem: Which electrolyte pattern is most characteristic of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)?

options.A: Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia
options.E: Hypercalcaemia with hypophosphataemia

explanation: Mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency causes renal sodium loss and potassium retention, producing hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia (with hypoglycaemia and sometimes hypercalcaemia). Secondary adrenal insufficiency preserves aldosterone, so hyperkalaemia is absent.
referenceText: Bornstein et al. 2016 (Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency) [21]

stem: A patient with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops sudden severe headache, visual field loss, ophthalmoplegia and hypotension. What is the most urgent treatment?

options.A: IV hydrocortisone, then neurosurgical assessment for decompression
options.D: Levothyroxine immediately, before any steroid replacement is given
options.E: Antiplatelet therapy

explanation: Pituitary apoplexy (haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary tumour) causes acute ACTH deficiency; hydrocortisone must be given immediately. Neurosurgical decompression is considered for severe visual deficits or reduced consciousness. Thyroid hormone must not be replaced before steroids.
referenceText: Bornstein et al. 2016 (Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency) [21]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with known adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 20 mg/day needs emergency laparotomy. What is the recommended perioperative glucocorticoid cover?

options.A: Dexamethasone 0.5 mg orally
options.C: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h by infusion or divided doses
options.E: Omit steroids on the day of surgery and restart the usual oral dose once eating normally

explanation: The 2020 guideline recommends 100 mg hydrocortisone IV at induction, then 200 mg/24 h (infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours) during major surgery and recovery, before returning to double the usual oral dose for 48 hours or longer. Missing stress doses risks adrenal crisis.
referenceText: Woodcock et al. 2020 (peri-operative glucocorticoids) [238]

stem: A young Asian man presents with acute flaccid quadriparesis after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Serum K+ is 1.9 mmol/L and he is tachycardic with a suppressed TSH. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Cautious potassium replacement plus propranolol, watching for rebound hyperkalaemia
options.C: Aggressive potassium replacement of 200 mmol over 2 hours via a central line, without beta-blockade
options.E: Insulin–glucose infusion

explanation: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis results from intracellular potassium shifts driven by thyroid hormone and catecholamines enhancing Na+/K+-ATPase activity. Total body potassium is normal, so large replacement causes rebound hyperkalaemia. Propranolol reverses the shift; definitive treatment of hyperthyroidism prevents recurrence.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Why is propylthiouracil sometimes preferred over methimazole in the acute treatment of thyroid storm?

options.A: It is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy without exception
options.C: It has a lower risk of hepatotoxicity
options.D: It additionally inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
options.E: It acts faster by blocking hormone release from the thyroid

explanation: PTU inhibits thyroid peroxidase and peripheral 5′-deiodinase, reducing T3 formation more rapidly. However, it carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity, so methimazole is preferred after the acute phase. Neither drug blocks release of preformed hormone; iodine does.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]

stem: After death by neurological criteria, a potential organ donor has polyuria of 500 mL/h, sodium 158 mmol/L and hypotension requiring noradrenaline. Which treatment addresses both problems?

options.A: Increasing the noradrenaline dose alone to maintain MAP above 65
options.B: Vasopressin infusion, with desmopressin for persistent polyuria
options.E: Hypertonic saline

explanation: Brain death causes posterior pituitary failure (diabetes insipidus) and loss of sympathetic tone. Low-dose vasopressin (e.g. up to 2.4 U/h) treats both vasodilatory hypotension and DI; desmopressin is added for persistent DI. Hypernatraemia should be corrected because it impairs liver graft function.
referenceText: Kotloff et al. 2015 (management of the potential organ donor) [118]; Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

stem: Which hormonal therapies may be used in haemodynamically unstable brain-dead donors?

options.A: Aldosterone antagonists
options.E: Calcitonin and parathyroid hormone

explanation: The SCCM/ACCP/AOPO consensus recommends vasopressin for vasoplegia and DI, corticosteroids (particularly to improve lung donation) and suggests thyroid hormone in unstable donors or those with reduced cardiac function. Evidence for thyroid hormone is mixed.
referenceText: Kotloff et al. 2015 (management of the potential organ donor) [118]

stem: Which is the most common precipitating factor of DKA in adults?

options.A: Hypothyroidism
options.E: Infection and insulin omission

explanation: Infection and inadequate or omitted insulin therapy are the most common precipitants. Others include new-onset diabetes, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, stroke, drugs (corticosteroids, SGLT2 inhibitors, antipsychotics) and substance use.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: Why is capillary or serum β-hydroxybutyrate preferred over urine ketone testing for monitoring DKA?

options.A: Urine tests detect β-hydroxybutyrate only
options.B: β-hydroxybutyrate is not elevated in DKA
options.C: Blood ketones cannot be measured at the bedside, so urine dipsticks are preferred for monitoring
options.D: Urine nitroprusside detects acetoacetate and acetone, not the predominant β-hydroxybutyrate
options.E: Urine ketones are more sensitive in early DKA

explanation: β-hydroxybutyrate is the main ketone in DKA (ratio to acetoacetate up to 10:1). Nitroprusside reactions do not detect it, so urine tests underestimate ketosis early and may appear to worsen during treatment as β-hydroxybutyrate converts to acetoacetate.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: In DKA, when is phosphate replacement recommended?

options.A: Routinely in all patients from the start of treatment, given as potassium phosphate with insulin
options.D: When phosphate is very low (e.g. <1.0 mg/dL) or with cardiac or respiratory dysfunction or anaemia
options.E: Never, because it causes hypocalcaemia only

explanation: Phosphate falls during insulin therapy, but routine replacement has not improved outcomes and may cause hypocalcaemia. It is recommended for severe hypophosphataemia or when complications such as respiratory muscle weakness, cardiac dysfunction or haemolytic anaemia are present.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: During treatment of HHS, serum sodium rises from 150 to 154 mmol/L over 6 hours while glucose falls from 50 to 35 mmol/L. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: Laboratory error
options.B: Failure of fluid therapy requiring insulin bolus
options.C: Dangerous hypernatraemia requiring a 5% dextrose bolus and a slower insulin infusion rate
options.E: An expected rise as glucose falls; effective osmolality is falling appropriately

explanation: As glucose falls, water moves into cells and sodium rises. JBDS states that a rise in sodium is acceptable if osmolality is falling at 3–8 mOsm/kg/h; switching to hypotonic fluids is considered only if osmolality stops falling despite adequate fluid balance. Sodium fall should not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
referenceText: Mustafa et al. 2023 (JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) [144]

stem: Which patients are at greatest risk of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia in the ICU?

options.A: Patients with stress hyperglycaemia on TPN that is running continuously without interruption
options.D: Patients with renal or liver failure, sepsis, or interrupted enteral or parenteral feeding
options.E: Patients with obesity only

explanation: Hypoglycaemia risk is higher with reduced insulin clearance (renal failure), impaired gluconeogenesis (liver failure, sepsis), adrenal insufficiency and when nutrition is stopped without adjusting insulin. Even brief hypoglycaemia is associated with increased mortality.
referenceText: NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]

stem: Which adverse effect of corticosteroids is most relevant in mechanically ventilated ICU patients?

options.A: Thrombocytosis causing arterial and venous thrombosis
options.D: Hyperglycaemia and ICU-acquired neuromyopathy, especially with NMBs
options.E: Hypoglycaemia

explanation: Corticosteroids cause hyperglycaemia, increased infection risk, delirium, gastrointestinal bleeding and myopathy; the risk of ICU-acquired weakness rises with concomitant neuromuscular blockade. Benefits in septic shock, ARDS and severe CAP generally outweigh risks at recommended doses.
referenceText: Chaudhuri et al. 2024 (SCCM corticosteroid update) [35]; Fan et al. 2014 (ATS ICU-acquired weakness) [66]

stem: A patient on long-term amiodarone develops thyrotoxicosis with low radioactive iodine uptake and no goitre. Which type and treatment are most likely?

options.A: Hashimoto thyroiditis, treated with lithium
options.B: Type 2 amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (destructive), treated with corticosteroids
options.E: Type 1 (iodine-induced hyperthyroidism), treated with radioactive iodine ablation

explanation: Type 2 AIT is a destructive thyroiditis in a normal gland, with low iodine uptake and low vascularity on Doppler; it responds to glucocorticoids. Type 1 occurs in underlying thyroid disease and is treated with thionamides (± perchlorate). Mixed forms are common.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: In a patient with septic shock requiring increasing vasopressors, should hydrocortisone be withheld until a cosyntropin test is performed?

options.A: No; start hydrocortisone on vasopressor requirement without waiting for testing
options.C: Yes; a random cortisol must be measured first and must be below 10 µg/dL before treatment
options.D: Hydrocortisone is contraindicated in septic shock
options.E: Yes; a cosyntropin test is mandatory first

explanation: SSC 2021 and CIRCI guidance do not require ACTH testing before hydrocortisone in septic shock; treatment is guided by persistent vasopressor requirement. Testing does not reliably predict benefit, and delays may be harmful. SSC 2026 continues to suggest IV corticosteroids in septic shock (conditional, low certainty).
referenceText: Annane et al. 2017 (CIRCI guideline) [9]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Why may a patient on enteral levothyroxine have rising TSH while receiving continuous nasogastric feeding?

options.A: Levothyroxine is inactivated by gastric acid suppression only when IV
options.B: Feeds reduce levothyroxine absorption; hold feeds around doses or use IV
options.E: Rising TSH is normal in critical illness and always requires dose doubling

explanation: Levothyroxine absorption is impaired by continuous enteral nutrition, calcium, iron, PPIs and sucralfate. Holding feeds 1 hour before and after dosing, or using IV levothyroxine (about 70–80% of the oral dose), maintains euthyroidism.
referenceText: Jonklaas et al. 2014 (ATA hypothyroidism) [106]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Why might bicarbonate remain low after ketonaemia has resolved in a patient treated for DKA with large volumes of 0.9% saline?

options.A: Respiratory alkalosis compensation
options.B: Hyperchloraemic normal anion gap acidosis from chloride load and ketoanion loss
options.D: Persistent ketoacidosis requiring higher fixed-rate insulin doses and IV bicarbonate
options.E: Development of lactic acidosis in all cases

explanation: During recovery, ketoanions (potential bicarbonate) are lost in urine and replaced by chloride, causing hyperchloraemic acidosis. This is usually benign and resolves with renal compensation; it should not be mistaken for ongoing ketoacidosis if ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]; Berend et al. 2014 (acid–base physiology) [17]

stem: A sedated ICU patient on an insulin infusion has a blood glucose of 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dL). What is the immediate management?

options.A: Give glucagon 1 mg IM and continue insulin
options.B: Stop insulin and give IV glucose (e.g. 100 mL 20% dextrose), rechecking within 15 minutes
options.C: Reduce the insulin infusion rate by half and recheck the blood glucose in about 4 hours
options.D: No action until glucose is below 2.2 mmol/L
options.E: Give oral glucose gel to the sedated patient

explanation: Hypoglycaemia in sedated patients is clinically silent and requires prompt IV glucose, stopping insulin and frequent rechecks. Glucagon is ineffective in glycogen-depleted states. The cause, such as interrupted feeding, should be identified and protocols reviewed.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]

subtopic: critical illness in chronic steroid users
stem: A patient on long-term prednisolone 10 mg/day is admitted with septic shock and cannot absorb enteral medications. What is the most appropriate steroid management?

options.A: Stop all steroids during critical illness
options.D: Continue prednisolone 10 mg via nasogastric tube regardless of absorption
options.E: IV hydrocortisone stress dosing (e.g. 50 mg every 6 hours or 200 mg/24 h)

explanation: Patients on long-term glucocorticoids (prednisolone ≥5 mg/day for more than 4 weeks) have suppressed HPA axes and are at risk of adrenal crisis during critical illness. IV hydrocortisone at stress doses is required until recovery, followed by tapering.
referenceText: Woodcock et al. 2020 (peri-operative glucocorticoids) [238]; Bornstein et al. 2016 (Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency) [21]
tags: critical illness in chronic steroid users

stem: After total thyroidectomy, a patient develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm with ionised calcium 0.85 mmol/L. What is the immediate treatment?

options.A: Furosemide
options.C: Magnesium sulfate infusion alone, because hypomagnesaemia is the underlying cause after surgery
options.E: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% over 10 minutes, then infusion and oral calcium/calcitriol

explanation: Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia within 24–48 hours. Symptomatic patients need IV calcium (gluconate preferred peripherally to reduce tissue injury), followed by infusion and oral calcium with calcitriol. Hypomagnesaemia should be corrected because it impairs PTH secretion.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What is the main mechanism of polyuria commonly seen after death by neurological criteria?

options.A: Cerebral salt wasting with hypovolaemia
options.B: Loss of posterior pituitary ADH secretion (central DI)
options.E: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from hypercalcaemia

explanation: Brain death causes failure of the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, leading to central DI in up to 80% of donors. Without treatment, hypovolaemia, hypernatraemia and electrolyte depletion compromise organ perfusion. Desmopressin and vasopressin are used along with fluid replacement.
referenceText: Kotloff et al. 2015 (management of the potential organ donor) [118]; Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

stem: A patient has glucose 45 mmol/L, effective osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, pH 7.18 and ketones 4.5 mmol/L. How should this be managed?

options.A: As euglycaemic DKA
options.C: As mixed DKA–HHS: fluids and fixed-rate insulin, avoiding rapid osmolality falls
options.D: As starvation ketosis with dextrose only
options.E: As pure HHS, withholding all insulin for 12 hours while giving hypotonic fluids only

explanation: Up to a third of hyperglycaemic crises have features of both DKA and HHS. Insulin is needed for ketoacidosis, but osmolality must be lowered gradually (3–8 mOsm/kg/h) to reduce cerebral oedema risk, with careful monitoring of electrolytes.
referenceText: Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]; Mustafa et al. 2023 (JBDS hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) [144]

stem: Which antipyretic is preferred in thyroid storm?

options.A: No antipyretic, because fever is protective
options.E: Paracetamol, with external cooling

explanation: Paracetamol and active cooling are recommended. Salicylates should be avoided because they displace T4 and T3 from thyroid-binding globulin, increasing free hormone levels.
referenceText: Ross et al. 2016 (ATA hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) [183]

stem: A patient has severe hypercalcaemia (3.8 mmol/L) due to a parathyroid adenoma, with AKI and confusion despite fluids and bisphosphonates. Which additional therapy can lower calcium in renal failure?

options.A: Oral vitamin D
options.B: Thiazide diuretics with fluid loading to increase urinary calcium excretion rapidly
options.E: Haemodialysis with low-calcium dialysate, or cinacalcet, pending parathyroidectomy

explanation: Severe primary hyperparathyroid crisis may be refractory and complicated by AKI. Dialysis with low-calcium dialysate rapidly lowers calcium; calcimimetics reduce PTH secretion. Definitive parathyroidectomy is curative. Thiazides raise calcium.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Why is subcutaneous insulin often unreliable in patients with shock receiving vasopressors?

options.A: Subcutaneous insulin is metabolised by noradrenaline
options.C: Peripheral vasoconstriction and oedema impair subcutaneous absorption
options.E: Subcutaneous insulin is contraindicated in mechanically ventilated patients

explanation: In shock, reduced skin perfusion and oedema make subcutaneous absorption erratic; IV insulin infusion with frequent glucose monitoring is preferred until haemodynamics stabilise.
referenceText: NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]; Compher et al. 2022 (ASPEN critical care nutrition) [38]

stem: Which glucose measurement source is least reliable in critically ill patients with shock and peripheral hypoperfusion?

options.A: Arterial blood on a blood gas analyser
options.B: Arterial blood sent to the central laboratory
options.D: Venous blood analysed in the laboratory
options.E: Venous blood on a blood gas analyser

explanation: Capillary glucose meters are affected by peripheral hypoperfusion, oedema, anaemia, hypoxia and some drugs, and may overestimate or underestimate glucose. Arterial or venous samples measured on blood gas or laboratory analysers are preferred in shock.
referenceText: NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient without known diabetes has glucose of 14 mmol/L during septic shock. Which test best distinguishes stress hyperglycaemia from previously undiagnosed diabetes?

options.A: Oral glucose tolerance test in the ICU
options.E: Random serum insulin

explanation: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over the preceding 2–3 months; a value of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more suggests pre-existing diabetes, whereas a normal value supports stress hyperglycaemia. It is unreliable after major blood loss or transfusion and in haemolysis.
referenceText: NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]; Umpierrez et al. 2024 (hyperglycaemic crises consensus) [219]

stem: Why may total serum cortisol be misleading in critically ill patients with severe hypoalbuminaemia?

options.A: Low cortisol-binding globulin and albumin lower total cortisol despite adequate free cortisol
options.B: Hypoalbuminaemia causes falsely high total cortisol
options.C: Free cortisol is unaffected by binding proteins in any situation, including severe sepsis and burns
options.E: Total cortisol cannot be measured below albumin 30 g/L

explanation: Most circulating cortisol is bound to cortisol-binding globulin and albumin, both of which fall in critical illness. Total cortisol may then underestimate free cortisol, risking overdiagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. Free cortisol assays are not widely available.
referenceText: Annane et al. 2017 (CIRCI guideline) [9]

stem: A patient deliberately injected 300 units of insulin glargine. After initial correction with IV dextrose, what is the expected course?

options.A: Recurrent hypoglycaemia for 24–72 hours or more, needing continuous dextrose and monitoring
options.E: Hypoglycaemia resolves permanently after a single 50 mL bolus of 50% dextrose at presentation

explanation: Large subcutaneous depots of long-acting insulin produce prolonged absorption and hypoglycaemia for days. Management includes continuous concentrated dextrose infusion, potassium monitoring and frequent glucose checks; surgical excision of the injection site has occasionally been used.
referenceText: Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A polyuric patient with hypernatraemia has urine osmolality of 150 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 450 mOsm/kg. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Osmotic diuresis
options.E: SIADH

explanation: A rise in urine osmolality of more than 50% after desmopressin indicates central DI (ADH deficiency with intact renal response); little or no rise indicates nephrogenic DI. Osmotic diuresis produces urine osmolality above about 300 mOsm/kg.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: A patient with polyuria has urine osmolality 600 mOsm/kg and glucose 650 mg/dL. What is the cause?

options.A: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

explanation: Polyuria with urine osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg is a solute (osmotic) diuresis; with glucose at 650 mg/dL, glycosuria is the cause. A water diuresis, from central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus or primary polydipsia, produces dilute urine, usually below 300 and often below 100 mOsm/kg. Other solute causes in the ICU are mannitol, urea after relief of obstruction or high-protein feeding, and saline loading. Treat the hyperglycaemia and replace the water deficit; the urine osmolality is the key discriminator.

stem: What MAP target is typical in donor management?

options.A: Lowest MAP that keeps urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h

explanation: After brain death, loss of sympathetic tone and diabetes insipidus cause vasodilatation and hypovolaemia. Donor management targets a MAP of at least 60–65 mmHg (often 60–100), with CVP 6–10 mmHg, urine output 0.5–3 mL/kg/h and normal lactate, using fluids, vasopressin as the preferred first vasopressor (it also treats DI), and noradrenaline if needed; high catecholamine doses can damage the heart. Hormone therapy (steroids, with thyroid hormone in unstable donors) is used. A MAP of 50 mmHg underperfuses organs, and 90 mmHg needs harmful vasopressor doses.

stem: For lung donation, which ventilation strategy improves lung procurement?

options.A: FiO2 1.0 continuously
options.B: Lung-protective ventilation with recruitment and PEEP
options.C: High tidal volume of 10–12 mL/kg to prevent atelectasis

explanation: In a multicentre RCT, Mascia et al. (JAMA 2010) found that a lung-protective strategy in potential brain-dead donors (tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg PBW, PEEP 8–10 cmH2O, closed-circuit suctioning and recruitment manoeuvres after disconnection, apnoea testing on CPAP) increased the proportion of donors whose lungs met criteria for transplantation (54% vs 27%) and the number of lungs transplanted. Tidal volumes of 10–12 mL/kg, zero PEEP and continuous FiO2 1.0 promote ventilator-induced injury, atelectasis and absorption collapse.

stem: A donor's PaO2/FiO2 is used in lung assessment. What value is acceptable?

options.A: >150 on PEEP 5 and FiO2 1.0

explanation: Standard ('ideal') donor lung criteria include a PaO2 above 300 mmHg on FiO2 1.0 and PEEP 5 cmH2O (P/F above 300), age under 55, a clear chest X-ray, less than 20 pack-years of smoking and no purulent secretions on bronchoscopy. Marginal lungs outside these criteria can be used after reassessment and recruitment, or after ex vivo lung perfusion. Ventilator management with recruitment and protective ventilation often improves the ratio. Values of 100–200 indicate significant lung injury and usually exclude donation without further assessment.
